the War on piracy in Brunei were anti-piracy operations against Pirates by Bruneian Empire. It was initiated in 17th century and intensified in the late 18th century as not only Brunei was one of the major targets of pirates. But it was one of the opponents of the Sulu Sultanate as they fought in the Twenty Years' War. It eventually ended in 1847 due to anti-piracy measures by James Brooke.
Background
Prior to the Twenty Years' War and the 17th century, piracy was tolerated by the Sultans of Brunei like Bolkiah. However in the aftermath of the Bruneian Civil War of 1660. It weaken Brunei for the next two centuries. Later the Twenty Years' War started when the Sultan of Sulu was instated by the British to control Manila in 1763. Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin who learned about the situation in Manila, he was displeased as Azim ud-Din I was a apostate. As a result, he commanded an attack on the Sulu Sultanate in Manila with his forces under the command of Pehin Orang Kaya Di-Gadong Seri Lela Awang Aliwaddin.
Anti-piracy operations
Brunei did nothing to defend the coast expect with a few defenses up even with pirates raiding coastal areas in northern Borneo for slaves as well as cut off trade into the Sultanate of Brunei. These attacks severely affected the economy of Brunei, leading to its decline. The Banguingui purportedly had a saying: "It is difficult to catch fish, but easy to catch Bruneians." until the arrival of James Brooke, Brunei and Sarawak started to aggressively stomp out piracy as a whole. Eventually piracy was pacified by James Brooke though it still continued in Sabah until the late 19th century. It was primarily pacified and ended major pirate raids in Borneo.
Aftermath
Despite curbing piracy in most of their territories, by the time Brunei crushed most of piracy activities, Brunei's trade routes were already taken by the Sulu Sultanate by 1725 and started to decline 30 years later in the 1870s and 1880s due to British interest in Brunei, eventually making it to sign the Treaty of Protection. Lasting until independence in 1984.
